wstep: This card describes how to dry asparagus in a dehydrator or oven at 140 °F (60 °C), after blanching.

akapity: Wash the asparagus thoroughly; halve large tips.
Blanch the asparagus for 4–5 minutes.
MSU rates asparagus as “poor to fair” for drying; MSU gives no reason for this rating.
Vegetables are blanched before drying to stop enzymes and increase the destruction of microorganisms.
Put at most 1 quart (about 0.95 l) of vegetables in a cheesecloth bag into boiling water; start timing when they go in and keep the water boiling the whole time.
Then cool the vegetables in very cold water for the same time as they were blanched, and drain them.

The blanching times on this card are for 3000–5000 feet (about 900–1500 m); CSU says they are slightly shorter at lower altitudes and slightly longer at higher altitudes or for large amounts of vegetables.

JarAtlas rule (cautious): do not shorten the times at lower altitudes, because blanching also helps destroy microorganisms; lengthen them slightly above about 1500 m or for large amounts of vegetables.
Arrange the pretreated vegetables on trays in a single or thin layer, no more than 1/2 inch (about 13 mm) deep.
Dry the vegetables at 140 °F (60 °C) in a dehydrator or oven.
Do not dry vegetables outdoors: dry them under the controlled conditions of an oven or dehydrator.
Do not use trays or screens made of galvanized mesh; also avoid copper and aluminium mesh.
Only use an oven if it can be set as low as 140 °F (60 °C); if it cannot go that low, the vegetables cook instead of drying.
In an oven, keep 140–150 °F (about 60–66 °C): place a calibrated oven thermometer on the rack or tray and check it every 2 hours throughout drying.
Leave the oven door open 2–3 inches (about 5–7.5 cm) so moisture can escape.
In a conventional oven, drying can take up to twice as long as in a dehydrator, depending on air circulation.
Dry the asparagus for 6–10 hours, until leathery to brittle.

When drying is complete, some pieces are moister than others because of their size and location during drying; conditioning distributes residual moisture evenly and lowers the chance of spoilage, so condition these dried pieces.
Put the cooled dried pieces in large plastic or glass containers about two-thirds full, cover lightly and keep them in a warm, dry, well-ventilated place for 4–10 days, stirring or shaking daily.
If beads of moisture form inside, return the food to the dehydrator, then condition it again.
Pack only completely cooled vegetables: warm dried food sweats, and that moisture can be enough for mould to grow.
Store the dried vegetables in clean, dry canning jars, plastic freezer containers with tight-fitting lids or plastic freezer bags.
Packaging must be food grade: do not use trash bags or plastic or fibreboard containers that previously held non-food items.
Pack amounts that can be used at one time: each opening exposes the dried food to air and moisture, which lowers quality and can lead to spoilage.
Vacuum packaging is not a preservation method by itself: removing oxygen increases the risk of botulism, and a product that needs refrigeration still needs it.
Store the dried vegetables in a cool, dry, dark place.
Dried vegetables keep about half as long as dried fruit: according to Clemson HGIC, about 6 months at 60 °F (about 15.6 °C) and 3 months at 80 °F (about 26.7 °C).

According to MSU, if you soak dried vegetables, cover them with cold water until they nearly regain their original texture (1/2–2 hours); if you soak them longer than 2 hours, keep them in the refrigerator.
Check the dried vegetables often (glass shows condensation); if they have taken up moisture but are not spoiled, use them at once or dry them again and repack them.
Throw away mouldy dried vegetables; also throw away any that smell off.
